title: SpaceX Fires Up Ship 42 as Flight 15 Targets First-Ever Starship Tower Catch
excerpt: SpaceX has completed static-fire tests on both stages of Starship Flight 15 — a full six-engine burn and a single-engine deorbit rehearsal on Ship 42, after a 33-engine firing of Booster 22 — ahead of a November launch that aims to catch both stages at the tower.
body:
• SpaceX has completed static-fire tests of Ship 42, the Starship upper stage for Flight 15: a full-duration six-engine burn and a single-engine firing simulating a deorbit burn.
  • Booster 22, the Super Heavy first stage, has also completed a 33-engine static fire, clearing both stages' engine tests.
  • Flight 15, expected in November, aims for a first: catching both the booster and the ship with the launch tower's chopstick arms. A ship has never been caught before.
  • The flight still needs FAA regulatory approval covering the ship's return and tower catch.

SpaceX has checked off the engine tests for its 15th Starship flight. The company conducted static-fire tests with the Flight 15 upper stage, known as Ship 42, on October 26 and 27 at its Starbase facility in South Texas, igniting the vehicle's Raptor engines while it remained anchored to the ground, according to Space.com's report. "Ship 42 static fires complete. The Starship preparing for Flight 15 performed a full duration, six-engine static fire, and fired a single Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn," SpaceX said in an October 28 post on X.

Why the single-engine burn matters

The six-engine firing, which ran for more than 60 seconds, tested the full propulsion system of the 171-foot ship. The separate single-engine test rehearsed the deorbit burn — the short firing that drops Starship out of orbit and aims its return. On Flight 14 in September, a single Raptor performed Starship's first-ever deorbit burn after the ship reached a stable low Earth orbit for the first time. On Flight 15, the precision of that burn matters far more, because it decides whether the ship comes back to Starbase or not.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cftUryKseIk

The catch attempt

Founder Elon Musk has said SpaceX will attempt to catch both stages of Flight 15 at the launch tower, provided regulators approve. Super Heavy boosters have been caught by the tower's chopstick arms before; a returning ship never has. The booster assigned to the flight, Booster 22, completed its own 33-engine static fire days before Ship 42's tests, and SpaceX crews have rehearsed ship handling by lifting the next vehicle, Ship 43, with the chopsticks. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell has said she expects the flight licence to include return-to-launch-site catches for both stages. Reports citing FAA planning information point to a possible November 12 target, though SpaceX has not confirmed a date.

https://x.com/SpaceX/status/2115476295169814978

"Ship 42 static fires complete. The Starship preparing for Flight 15 performed a full duration, six-engine static fire, and fired a single Raptor engine to simulate a deorbit burn."

— SpaceX, on X

What comes next

Flight 15 will be the fourth flight of the Starship V3 configuration, the taller and more powerful version of the 408-foot stack that SpaceX began flying this year. Preparations are already running in parallel for Flight 16: its ship, Ship 43, has completed cryogenic testing and was lifted by the tower's chopsticks in a handling rehearsal while Ship 42 was out at the test stand. Musk has rated the ship-catch attempt "more likely than not" to succeed — an unusually candid marker for a manoeuvre no rocket programme has ever completed. Ship 42 returns to the Megabay for final outfitting and loading of its Starlink V3 satellite payload while SpaceX awaits the FAA licence. A successful double catch would be the strongest evidence yet that Starship — the largest rocket ever flown — can be recovered whole and reflown, the capability on which SpaceX's plans for high-cadence launches, lunar missions and Mars cargo all depend.
